newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Taleban rattles nerves in north Afghanistan.
newsitem.headline: Taleban rattles nerves in north Afghanistan.

text.p: At first sight it was business as usual in Mazar-i-Sharif, where veiled women shoppers bargained for boxes of green tea and cages full of chickens in the main bazaar on Monday.

Taleban commanders and aid workers said the Taleban seized the town of Jabal os-Siraj at the foot of the strategic Panjsher Valley on Monday and it has set nerves on edge in the northern territory around Mazar-i-Sharif, an important trading centre controlled by warlord Rashid Dostum.
Officials with Dostum's well-armed Jumbish-i-Milli faction said they were ready to fight if the Taleban pushed further north.
"We don't want to join this war," said a senior Jumbish official who declined to be named. "But if they (the Taleban) attack, we would defend ourselves."

Students were nervous about what would happen to them if the Islamic Taleban arrived, and the fall of the afghani currency -- from 23,000 to the dollar on Sunday to 27,500 on Monday -- spoke volumes about the political uncertainty gripping the town.

"Before, we did not think they (Taleban) would be able to take Kabul. Now we see they are very strong," said Isabel, a 22-year-old student of English at the university, one of just a handful functioning in Afghanistan.
Asked what would happen if the Taleban took Mazar-i-Sharif, she said: "We would have to live at home like slaves, we could not even go to the bazaar."
Male student Nasir Bessed, 24, agreed. "It is not written in the Qur'an to ban women's rights and stop them working beside their Moslem brothers," he said.
The Taleban in Kabul have issued orders barring women from workplaces and told them not to leave their homes without wearing the Islamic "hejab" veil.
Eyewitnesses in the capital said at least four women had been beaten in public for violating Islamic dress codes by Taleban fighters wielding long chains on Sunday.

Mazar-i-Sharif, some 300 km (200 miles) northwest of Kabul, has thousands of well-armed men but has largely stayed out of the confrontation between ousted president Burhanuddin Rabbani's government and the Taleban.
The city is a large trading centre for electronic goods destined for markets in former Soviet Central Asia, including the television sets now frowned upon by the Taleban movement.

The Taleban captured Jabal os-Saraj on Monday after their spectacular capture of Kabul on Friday. Some reports said that Dostum had reinforced troops on the Salang pass northwest of Kabul, but no confirmation was available.
Another Jumbish official said the faction had strengthened its positions along the Salang highway 30 km (20 miles) northwest of Jabal-us-Saraj, earlier this month.
Dostum's Jumbish faction, or the "National Islamic movement of Afghanistan", controls six provinces in the north of Afghanistan.
Jumbish officials said Dostum had left Mazar-i-Sharif on Friday but declined to say where he had gone.
Rumours abound of meetings between Dostum and faction leaders who sided with deposed president Rabbani but they have not been confirmed.
